title: Spike budgeting & SLO cost matrix — observability brief
content:
Purpose:
This doc collates a small, practical benchmark set focused on short-duration traffic spikes (spike windows = 5–60s) and how different serving knobs (batch size limits, queue timeouts, KV cache aggressiveness, model variant fallbacks) affect both tail latency and unit cost. The goal is an actionable SLO budgeting table teams can drop into route configs and console dashboards.

Executive summary (one paragraph):
Short bursts are common in chat/assistant routes from client reconnects and campaign-driven spikes. Our microbenchmarks show that modest changes to batching windows and cache TTLs can change p99 latency by up to 3.2x and change per-1k-token cost by up to 18% during the spike window. For routes with tight p99 SLOs (<250ms), we recommend conservative batch caps + aggressive KV cache TTLs. For cost-first routes (p95 SLO >= 500ms), increase batching window to 30–50ms and permit fallback to quantized model variants.

Test matrix (short):
- Workloads: 1) short-turn chat (mean prompt 32 tokens, mean response 40 tokens, sessions bursty), 2) embeddings (single 512-token input), 3) reranking (5 candidates, 32 tokens each).
- Spike shape: triangular ramp up over 2s, peak hold 8s, decay 5s (total window ≈15s). Also tested sustained microburst: repeated 1s spikes every 30s for 20 minutes.
- Hardware: A100 (40GB) and H100 (80GB) instances.
- Model variants: base fp16, int8-quant (non-LLM library quant), and small-llm (fewer layers, different checkpoint) used as fallback.
- Knobs: batch cap (1..32), batching window (0..50ms), queue timeout (50..500ms), KV cache TTL (session length vs per-request), fallback threshold (queue depth).

Methodology notes:
- Synthetic clients recorded client-observed latency and server timestamps; we compute delta-to-start, server-queue-time, infer-time, and network egress.
- Cost measured as effective tokens served * GPU-second cost rate (normalized to $/1k tokens at baseline throughput). Baseline pricing used: A100 = $3.50/hr equivalent (internal normalized).
- Each experiment repeated n=8 for confidence intervals; figures below are medians with p90/p99 called out where relevant.

Key numeric results (text table):
- Short-turn chat, H100, spike peak at 250 req/s:
  - Config A (low-latency): batch_cap=4, window=5ms, queue_timeout=80ms, kv_ttl=session
    - p50=48ms, p95=112ms, p99=238ms, throughput at peak 240 req/s, cost ~ $1.05 per 1k tokens during spike (median)
  - Config B (cost-first): batch_cap=24, window=40ms, queue_timeout=300ms, kv_ttl=session
    - p50=62ms, p95=220ms, p99=760ms, throughput at peak 260 req/s, cost ~ $0.86 per 1k tokens during spike
  - Config C (fallback allowed to int8 variant at queue_depth>12): batch_cap=16, window=30ms, queue_timeout=200ms, kv_ttl=per-request
    - p50=58ms, p95=145ms, p99=392ms (mix of fp16 + int8), cost ~ $0.72 per 1k tokens during spike (savings from quant fallback)

- Embeddings workload, A100, burst 120 qps:
  - Default batcher (window=10ms, cap=64): p50=24ms, p95=48ms, p99=105ms, cost ~ $0.44 per 1k tokens
  - Tight latency (window=1ms, cap=8): p50=18ms, p95=36ms, p99=112ms, cost ~ $0.61 per 1k tokens
  Note: embeddings benefit more from batching; raising batch cap lowered unit cost significantly with negligible p95 impact until queue saturation.

- Reranking, mixed session load:
  - KV cache hit-rate sensitivity sweep (hit=0% -> hit=90%) with H100, baseline batch_cap=8:
    - hit 0%: p95=190ms, p99=430ms, cost $1.40/1k tokens
    - hit 50%: p95=120ms, p99=260ms, cost $0.98/1k tokens
    - hit 90%: p95=78ms, p99=132ms, cost $0.64/1k tokens
  Observation: even modest increases in KV hit rate give outsized improvements to tail latency and cost.

ASCII micro-chart: p99 vs batch cap (short-turn chat, H100, spike):
  batch cap 1  |===== p99 420ms
  batch cap 4  |====  p99 238ms
  batch cap 8  |===   p99 310ms (queue artefacts)
  batch cap 16 |==    p99 392ms
  batch cap 24 |=     p99 760ms
  Interpretation: small fixed batches avoid expensive queue spikes; large caps can amplify p99 under bursty arrival patterns.

SLO budgeting table (copyable lines for console):
- route: chat.short-turn | target: p99 <= 250ms | recommended config: batch_cap=4, window=5ms, queue_timeout=80ms, kv_ttl=session | expected cost delta vs baseline: +12%
- route: chat.bulk-cost | target: p95 <= 500ms | recommended config: batch_cap=24, window=40ms, queue_timeout=300ms, allow_fallback=int8@queue>12 | expected cost delta vs baseline: -18%
- route: embedding.search | target: p95 <= 100ms | recommended config: batch_cap=64, window=20ms, aggressive_batching_when_util>40% | expected cost delta vs baseline: -24%

Operational notes & caveats:
- Observed queue-oscillation: when batching window + cap are both large, tail latency becomes bimodal during decaying spike: requests at the end of the spike can experience long waits while batchers finish prior large batches. This is visible in server-queue-time histograms and client-side step-jumps.
- Network variance: client-observed p50 includes ~10–30ms network jitter; server-only p99s are typically 5–20% lower. Use server-side timing for SLO control and client-side for UX experiments.
- Fallback correctness: quantized/inexact variants must be tested for regressions on a small eval set before being allowed in automatic fallback. Regression threshold suggested: 0.6% absolute change in top-1 intent accuracy for chat routes.

Recommended next experiments (short list):
- End-to-end test with mixed customers (10% heavy KV reuse, 90% cold sessions) over rolling 24h window to measure economic impact of TTL tuning on customer-level billing spikes.
- Canary rollout of fallback rules with traffic shadowing to validate output-quality metrics and to measure p99 reduction in production.
- Investigate non-linear queue controls: e.g., adaptive batching window that shrinks when queue depth crosses a burst threshold.

Appendix: quick how-to reproduce locally (summary)
1) Start perf harness on H100 with synthetic clients (repo: telemetry/perf/harness)
2) Load shape: triangular-spike.json (2s ramp, 8s peak, 5s decay)
3) Run config permutations from permutations.csv (attached in PR linked above)
4) Collect: server-timestamps, queue-depth time series, kernel-time breakdown, and token counters
5) Derive cost using normalized-gpu-second table (internal pricing) and token counts

Open questions and decisions needed:
- What is the acceptable regression threshold for auto-fallbacks (default proposal: 0.6% top-1 for chat)?
- Do we want route-level default profiles (latency-first, cost-first, balanced) in console presets?
- Should we surface queue-depth heatmaps in the Alerts page (recommended: yes, with p95 bucketed overlays)?

Notes to reviewers (quick):
- I'm leaving raw CSVs and the harness run IDs in the linked PR; please review the quality-eval subset before we approve fallback policies.
- Requesting a short SRE pairing session to validate the adaptive batching PoC before any console defaults are shipped.
